ECE 6390 / Digital signals

The modem signal chain

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows how information rate, coding, modulation and pulse shape determine the transmitted waveform together.

Information bits enter a channel encoder. Code rate Rc is information bits per coded bit, so Rcoded = Rb/Rc. An M-point modulation alphabet maps log₂M coded bits into each symbol, giving Rs = Rb/(Rc log₂M).

A combined raised-cosine response with rolloff α has total occupied passband width approximately (1 + α)Rs. Its pulse shape satisfies the Nyquist zero-ISI condition at the intended symbol times. Suitable root-raised-cosine transmit and matched-receive filters can form that combined response.

Changing constellation order changes bit loading and normalized point spacing; changing rolloff changes spectrum and pulse shape. The rate chain alone does not predict bit errors or amplifier behavior. Source compression is already included in the input, and extra pilots, framing, and synchronization overhead are omitted.

Example

At 6 Mbit/s information rate, code rate 3/4, 16-QAM, and rolloff 0.25, the coded rate is 8 Mbit/s, symbol rate is 2 Mbaud, and total RF width is approximately 2.5 MHz.

Model and course sources

    Practice

    1. With information rate, constellation, and rolloff fixed, how do coded rate, symbol rate, and RF width change when code rate moves from 1 to 1/2?

    The encoder now sends two coded bits for each information bit.

    All three double. The added coding redundancy requires a greater downstream rate if the information input stays unchanged.

    2. Why does halving symbol rate by increasing constellation order fail to establish unchanged link reliability?

    Compare point separation at the same average symbol energy.

    More points generally sit closer together relative to noise. A rate and bandwidth saving must be evaluated alongside the modulation's required received quality, coding, and hardware constraints.
